title: She Came Back. She Lost. But Serena Williams at 44 on Centre Court Was the Moment Wimbledon Needed.
excerpt: Four years after her last singles match, Williams accepted a wildcard, fought through a second-set tiebreak for the ages, and bowed out to 20-year-old Maya Joint 6-3, 6-7(6), 6-3 — then confirmed she'll play doubles with Venus on Thursday.
body:
She walked out to a standing ovation. Fifteen thousand people on their feet at Centre Court. A montage of her greatest Wimbledon moments had just played on the giant screen — seven of her 23 Grand Slam singles titles were won right here — and the crowd rose before she'd hit a single ball.

Serena Williams, 44 years old, four years away from competitive singles tennis, mother of two, had accepted a wildcard to play Wimbledon one more time. And on a cool London evening that required the Centre Court roof to be closed, she reminded the world why she is, by any reasonable measure, the greatest female tennis player who has ever lived.

She also lost. Maya Joint, a 20-year-old Australian ranked 87th in the world, beat Williams 6-3, 6-7(6), 6-3 in two hours and 22 minutes — earning the biggest win of her young career on the stage Williams once owned.

## A Second Set for the Ages

The first set belonged to Joint. After the games levelled at 3-3, the Australian won three straight to take it 6-3. Williams looked rusty, her movement half a step behind, her groundstrokes finding errors more often than winners — 30 unforced groundstroke errors by the end of the night.

But the second set was peak Serena. The serve — still a weapon at 44, still producing seven aces across the match — began finding its spots. She clawed her way into a tiebreak, and when Joint had a match point at 6-5 in the breaker, Williams saved it. The crowd erupted. She took the tiebreak 8-6 and suddenly Centre Court believed.

It was not to be. The third set revealed what four years away from singles tennis costs, even the greatest. Williams won just three games as Joint, now free of the paralysing awe she'd carried into the match, played clean, decisive tennis to close it out.

"It was really great to be back at Wimbledon," Williams said afterward, smiling. "I never expected to be here. The atmosphere was amazing. Walking out was amazing. I definitely relished it and missed it and enjoyed the moment more than anything."



> **""It was really great to be back at Wimbledon," Williams said afterward, smiling."**


## Joint: Born After the Dynasty Began

Maya Joint was not born when Serena Williams won the first seven of her 23 Grand Slam singles titles. She is the future of women's tennis, and beating the greatest of all time on Centre Court is the kind of career-defining moment that changes trajectories.

"I really don't know what to say right now. I don't know what just happened," Joint said, visibly emotional. "I didn't get much sleep last night, I was up until 2 a.m. just thinking about it. Walking out today, I forgot the warm-up. My legs weren't moving."

"She has so much aura, she's such a legend. I've been dreaming about this since I was a little kid, so this is pretty crazy."


![Second Set — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/f/f9/Second_Set.jpg)


Joint will face Filipino 29th seed Alexandra Eala in the second round.

## Not Done Yet: Venus Awaits

Williams's singles run at Wimbledon 2026 may have ended in the first round, but her tournament is far from over. She and her older sister Venus Williams are entered in the women's doubles — a pairing that has won 14 Grand Slam doubles titles and three Olympic gold medals across a career spanning three decades.

Their first-round doubles match is scheduled for Thursday, July 2. It may well be the last time the Williams sisters take the court together at a Grand Slam. The doubles tournament offers them a gentler format to say goodbye properly — and knowing the sisters, one more chance to compete.

## Stan Wawrinka's Farewell

Williams was not the only legend bidding Centre Court adieu on Tuesday. Stan Wawrinka, 41, three-time Grand Slam champion, played his final Wimbledon match — a gruelling four-set tiebreak marathon against Matteo Berrettini, losing 6-7(7), 7-6(16), 7-6(7), 7-6(5). The second-set tiebreak alone, at 18-16, was the longest in Wimbledon history.

The Swiss veteran waved to the crowd as he walked off for the last time. An era is ending on the grass.

## Why This Matters for Indian Tennis Fans

India's relationship with tennis has always been shaped by its champions — Leander Paes, Mahesh Bhupathi, Sania Mirza — and by the global icons those champions competed alongside. Serena Williams is one of the most-followed athletes in India, a country that watched her dominate for two decades and celebrated her rivalries with the same intensity as cricket's greatest battles.

With no Indian singles player at Wimbledon this year — Yuki Bhambri is the lone Indian presence in the men's doubles draw, and junior Revathi Paparkar carries India's hopes in the girls' tournament — Serena's comeback was the kind of cross-cultural sporting moment that NRIs in the US, UK, and beyond tuned in for.

For Indian-Americans especially, Williams's story of comeback and defiance at 44 echoes a sporting philosophy they know well from cricket: champions don't retire easily. Sachin Tendulkar played his 200th Test at 40. MS Dhoni returned from months of silence at 38 to captain CSK to another IPL title. And now Serena, at 44, walked onto Centre Court one more time — not because she needed to, but because the competitor in her wouldn't let it go.

**Sources:** Reuters, The Sun, Fox News, Sky Sports

**How to watch Wimbledon in the US:** ESPN and ESPN+ carry full coverage. In India, the tournament is broadcast on Star Sports and streamed on JioHotstar.
nri_angle: Serena's comeback resonates with Indian fans who watched legends like Tendulkar and Dhoni return beyond their prime — and NRIs following Wimbledon amid India's singles drought adds emotional weight.
